marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q001.takeaway: The aortic valve surface marking is beside the sternum in the left third intercostal space; auscultation is at the right second intercostal space.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q001.displayText:
The aortic valve surface marking is beside the sternum in the left third intercostal space; auscultation is at the right second intercostal space.

The surface marking of the aortic valve is beside the sternum in the left third intercostal space. The source figure shows the relation of the cardiac valves to the thoracic cage.
emphasis: The aortic valve surface marking is beside the sternum in the left third intercostal space; auscultation is at the right second intercostal space

rationales.a: The sternal end of left third cartilage is the deeper anatomical projection, not the surface marking used in this question.
rationales.b: The right third cartilage is not the valve surface marking.
rationales.d: The right third intercostal space is not the aortic valve surface landmark.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q002.takeaway: The mitral valve lies behind the left fourth costal cartilage near its sternal end.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q002.displayText:
The mitral valve lies behind the left fourth costal cartilage near its sternal end.

The mitral valve orifice is level with the left half of the sternum opposite the left fourth costal cartilage. The source represents it by a line approximately 3 cm long descending to the right.
emphasis: The mitral valve lies behind the left fourth costal cartilage near its sternal end

rationales.b: The right fourth cartilage is not the mitral valve projection.
rationales.c: The midclavicular fourth intercostal space is the auscultation area, not the valve’s surface marking.
rationales.d: The left third intercostal space is too superior for the mitral valve projection.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q003.takeaway: Left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve beneath the aortic arch and cause hoarseness.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q003.displayText:
Left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve beneath the aortic arch and cause hoarseness.

The base of the heart is formed mainly by the left atrium, so left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness. The base is quadrilateral, directed posteriorly, and consists mainly of the left atrium with a small part of the right atrium and the proximal portions of the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and pulmonary veins. In the supine position it lies approximately opposite T5-T8. The apex is formed by the left ventricle in the fifth intercostal space. The sternocostal surface is formed by right atrium, right ventricle and left ventricle; the diaphragmatic and left surfaces are mainly left ventricle, and the right surface is mainly right atrium.
emphasis: Left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve beneath the aortic arch and cause hoarseness

rationales.a: Right atrial enlargement does not lie adjacent to the left recurrent laryngeal loop.
rationales.c: Right ventricle forms the anterior heart surface and is not the chamber near the left nerve.
rationales.d: Left ventricle is not the chamber whose base compresses the nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q004.takeaway: The marked right cardiac border corresponds chiefly to the right atrium.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q004.displayText:
The marked right cardiac border corresponds chiefly to the right atrium.

The marked region corresponds to the surface marking of the right atrium. The source describes the right cardiac border as a laterally convex line from the third to the sixth right costal cartilage approximately 1-2 cm lateral to the sternal edge. It also reviews the other borders: upper border from the second left costal cartilage to the third right costal cartilage, inferior border from the sixth right costal cartilage to the apex, and left border from the apex superomedially to the second left costal cartilage.
emphasis: The marked right cardiac border corresponds chiefly to the right atrium

rationales.a: The thoracic duct is posterior in the mediastinum, not the anterior right heart border.
rationales.c: Bronchopulmonary segments are lung regions, not cardiac surface markings.
rationales.d: The hilum is the lung root, not a heart border.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q005.takeaway: The right ventricle lies immediately behind the sternum and is most exposed to anterior chest-wall trauma.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q005.displayText:
The right ventricle lies immediately behind the sternum and is most exposed to anterior chest-wall trauma.

The right ventricle is most likely to be injured because it forms the major part of the sternocostal surface and lies directly posterior to the sternum, separated from the anterior thoracic wall mainly by the pericardium.
emphasis: The right ventricle lies immediately behind the sternum and is most exposed to anterior chest-wall trauma

rationales.a: The left atrium is posterior and shielded by other structures.
rationales.b: The left ventricle forms much of the left/inferior heart border, not the most anterior chamber.
rationales.d: The right atrium forms the right border but is less anterior than the right ventricle.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q006.takeaway: The crista terminalis in the right atrium gives origin to pectinate muscles that extend through the auricle.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q006.displayText:
The crista terminalis in the right atrium gives origin to pectinate muscles that extend through the auricle.

The ridge is the crista terminalis in the right atrium. It extends along the atrial wall from the opening of the superior vena cava toward the inferior vena cava, corresponds externally to the sulcus terminalis, and gives origin to the pectinate muscles. It separates the smooth posterior part of the right atrium from the rough anterior part; the venae cavae open into the smooth posterior region.
emphasis: The crista terminalis in the right atrium gives origin to pectinate muscles that extend through the auricle

rationales.b: Left atrium has pectinate muscle mainly in its auricle, but the named ridge is the right atrial crista terminalis.
rationales.c: Right ventricle has trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles, not pectinate muscles.
rationales.d: Left ventricle has trabeculae carneae, not the atrial pectinate ridge.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q007.takeaway: The right atrium forms most of the anatomical right border of the heart.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q007.displayText:
The right atrium forms most of the anatomical right border of the heart.

The right border of the heart is formed by the right atrium. The source summarizes the cardiac borders as: right - right atrium; left - mostly left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage; inferior - mostly right ventricle with a small contribution from left ventricle; upper - left atrium together with the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
emphasis: The right atrium forms most of the anatomical right border of the heart

rationales.b: Right ventricle contributes mainly to the anterior surface and inferior border.
rationales.c: SVC contributes to the upper mediastinal contour but not most of the cardiac right border.
rationales.d: IVC enters the right atrium inferiorly and does not form the cardiac border.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q008.takeaway: After foramen ovale closure, septum primum forms the valve/floor of the fossa ovalis and septum secundum forms its raised rim.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q008.displayText:
After foramen ovale closure, septum primum forms the valve/floor of the fossa ovalis and septum secundum forms its raised rim.

The fetal interatrial communication is the foramen ovale. After closure it forms the fossa ovalis. The floor of the fossa ovalis is the remnant of the septum primum, while its limbus is derived from the septum secundum.
emphasis: After foramen ovale closure, septum primum forms the valve/floor of the fossa ovalis and septum secundum forms its raised rim

rationales.b: Septum secundum forms the limbus (rim), not the floor/valve.
rationales.c: Endocardial cushions contribute to atrioventricular septation, not the fossa ovalis floor.
rationales.d: The tricuspid orifice is unrelated to the interatrial septal remnant.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q010.takeaway: The triangle of Koch is bounded by tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet and coronary sinus; posterior leaflet is not a boundary.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q010.displayText:
The triangle of Koch is bounded by tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet and coronary sinus; posterior leaflet is not a boundary.

The posterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve is not a boundary of the triangle of Koch. The atrioventricular node lies centrally within the triangle of Koch on the smooth posterior part of the right atrium. The source gives its boundaries as the coronary sinus, tendon of Todaro and the septal cusp/leaflet of the tricuspid valve.
emphasis: The triangle of Koch is bounded by tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet and coronary sinus; posterior leaflet is not a boundary

rationales.a: Tendon of Todaro forms the superior boundary.
rationales.b: The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve forms the anterior boundary.
rationales.d: The coronary sinus opening forms the inferior/posterior boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q011.takeaway: The SA node lies near the SVC opening at the upper end of the crista terminalis, not at the right border of the ascending aorta.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q011.displayText:
The SA node lies near the SVC opening at the upper end of the crista terminalis, not at the right border of the ascending aorta.

The false statement is that the sinoatrial node is located at the right border of the ascending aorta. The source places the SA node at the opening of the superior vena cava into the right atrium. It contains specialized nodal cardiac muscle and acts as the pacemaker, is supplied by atrial branches of the right coronary artery, and its action potential lacks phases 1 and 2.
emphasis: The SA node lies near the SVC opening at the upper end of the crista terminalis, not at the right border of the ascending aorta

rationales.b: SA-node tissue is specialized nodal cardiac muscle.
rationales.c: The SA node is commonly supplied by the RCA atrial branch.
rationales.d: Nodal action potentials lack the fast-response phase 1 and plateau phase 2.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q012.takeaway: The ascending aorta lies anterior to the transverse pericardial sinus and can be clamped through it.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q012.displayText:
The ascending aorta lies anterior to the transverse pericardial sinus and can be clamped through it.

The aorta lies anterior to the transverse pericardial sinus. The source explains that serous pericardial reflections form one tube around the aorta and pulmonary trunk and another around the venae cavae and pulmonary veins. The oblique sinus is a J-shaped recess posterior to the left atrium, while the transverse sinus is the passage between these arterial and venous reflections. The aorta and pulmonary trunk lie anterior to the transverse sinus, with the superior vena cava and atria posterior. This permits clamping of the great arterial outflow vessels during cardiac surgery.
emphasis: The ascending aorta lies anterior to the transverse pericardial sinus and can be clamped through it

rationales.b: Pulmonary artery also lies anterior to the sinus, but the vessel specified in the source is the aorta.
rationales.c: IVC enters inferiorly and is not anterior to the transverse sinus.
rationales.d: SVC lies posterior to the transverse sinus.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q013.takeaway: The left ventricle has two papillary muscles: anterolateral and posteromedial.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q013.displayText:
The left ventricle has two papillary muscles: anterolateral and posteromedial.

The left ventricle contains two papillary muscles: anterior and posterior. The source contrasts this with the right ventricle, which has three papillary muscles: anterior, posterior and septal.
emphasis: The left ventricle has two papillary muscles: anterolateral and posteromedial

rationales.b: Three is the typical number of papillary muscles in the right ventricle, not left.
rationales.c: Five exceeds the usual left-ventricular pair.
rationales.d: Eight is not the normal left-ventricular anatomy.

marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q014.takeaway: Purkinje fibers are specialized cardiac muscle cells that conduct impulses rapidly through ventricular myocardium.
marrow__ANAT_CH45_Q014.displayText:
Purkinje fibers are specialized cardiac muscle cells that conduct impulses rapidly through ventricular myocardium.

Purkinje fibers are modified cardiac muscle fibers. They form a subendocardial conducting network; excitation proceeds from the endocardial surface toward the epicardium.
emphasis: Purkinje fibers are specialized cardiac muscle cells that conduct impulses rapidly through ventricular myocardium

rationales.a: They are not modified nerve fibers; they are cardiomyocytes.
rationales.d: They are cellular conducting tissue rather than fibrous connective tissue.
